title: Shabbat morning
hookLine: in a synagogue, a park, or at home with the portion
tomorrow: two schools argue over one word in the Havdalah blessing. which?

cards: Before answering a long, tricky message, plenty of people read it twice: once for what it says, once for what it means. The Talmud asks something like that of the weekly Torah portion, with a twist.
Read it twice in the original, it says, and then once more, in a translation. That's the puzzle. Why read the same verses twice, and why a third time in another language?

teach.h: TWICE THE VERSE, ONCE THE TARGUM.
teach.b: The rule is in the Talmud's tractate Berakhot: a person should complete their portions along with the community, the scripture twice and the targum once.

The Targum is the old Aramaic translation, the one ordinary people once understood. The Talmud even attaches a promise: whoever completes the portions with the community has their days and years lengthened.
So, the puzzle. The text doesn't explain the numbers, so readers have offered answers. One: the first reading is for the words, the second is for hearing yourself in them.
Another: a text only pronounced isn't yet a text understood, and the translation is the way in.
Later law codes allowed a commentary like Rashi's to stand in for the Targum, which tells you what the third reading is for: understanding. It's an old instinct.

teach.h: TO HEAR IT, THEN TO UNDERSTAND.
teach.b: In Nehemiah, when Ezra reads the Torah to the gathered people, the readers give the sense, so that everyone understands what they hear. And notice the phrase, with the community.
Every week, Jews in many places read the same portion.

teach.h: A SCROLL, A BENCH, A KITCHEN.
teach.b: In a synagogue, it's read aloud from the scroll. In a park, from a printed book on a bench. At home, at the kitchen table before anyone's up.
What stays is the portion, and that you read it in step with everyone else reading it that week.
One to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud's rule builds a translation right into the reading.

how: On Shabbat morning the week's portion is read aloud from the Torah scroll in synagogue; some also review it at home during the week or on Shabbat, reading the verses twice and a translation or commentary once.

games.q: your friend wants to follow the weekly portion but reads no Hebrew, and thinks that rules her out. what does the Talmud's rule suggest?
o: the rule builds in a translation; reading in a language she knows is part of it.
she should wait until she has learned Hebrew, so that it counts.
hearing it once in synagogue is enough; reading isn't needed.
games.why: twice the verse, once the Targum: understanding is part of the reading. later codes even allowed a commentary in place of the Targum.

practice: Find this week's portion, or any short passage of Torah you have on hand. Read one verse twice, slowly, then say it once in your own plain words. Write that plain version by hand, one line: your own small targum.
